name: Esther Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, describe a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy furniture and homeware, sofas, tables, lamps, kitchenware, for a distributor that supplies about four hundred independent furniture and home shops. Mornings are catalogues and samples, and I fly out twice a year to the trade fairs in Italy and Poland. I'm the one who decides what a hundred shop owners will have on their floors next spring. I'm good at it. What wears me out is the big online marketplaces, which squeeze our shops and then squeeze us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, a few small helpers and that's all. At church coffee I'd say people get over-excited about every new machine. I wouldn't post anything online, that's not my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel calm about my job. Choosing what a shop owner wants for spring is about taste and trust, and I've built that over thirty years. What I do worry about is the marketplaces, and that Martin's workshop has had a poor two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep using the planning tool for forecasts now and then, and keep flying to the fairs. I'd save a little more each month and put some toward Martin's workshop, perhaps a new saw he's wanted. I'd keep my church choir on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. It's not exciting, but it's comfortable. I like a world where what I know still counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay calm. What would you still be watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The online marketplaces. Our shops are losing sales to the online marketplaces, and if the shops go, we go. That's a bigger threat to my job than any computer program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the tools more or less in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it for sales forecasts. It's right about two-thirds of the time. I check each forecast against the shop owners' own feel. If they disagree, I trust the shop owners.

say: At work I'd say a **few helpers** and that's all.
At church I'd say people get over-excited about every **new machine**.
think: Choosing what shops want rests on **taste and trust** built over thirty years, so I'm calm.
My worry is **online marketplaces** and Martin's weak workshop income.
do: Keep using the **planning tool** for forecasts now and then.
Save more and help buy Martin a **new saw**.
Keep singing in the **church choir** on Thursdays.
feel: **Settled**, comfortable, in a world where experience counts.
S0.quote: Our shops are losing sales to the online marketplaces, and if the shops go, we go.
fieldNote: She is **calm** because her job is built on taste and trust, and her real threat is the marketplaces squeezing her customers.
She **checks the tool** against shop owners' feel, a steady, evidence-led habit.

steps.text: Use the sales forecast tool now and then and check it
Save a bit more and help buy Martin a new saw
Keep visiting the trade fairs and shop owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real change and we need to prepare the young for it. At work I'd say, let's test it properly on small orders. At church I'd say we should help people who lose work, and the young need apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit uneasy. Much of buying is the thinking work on the card: comparing prices, checking catalogues, planning orders. Software will do that part. The taste part is harder for it, but a manager might not see the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, once I've seen they work, and I'd try them on a small range first. I'd focus on the part where I'm best, spotting what customers will like. And I'd save more, say 350 a month, in case the firm cuts a senior buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I like the work and I'm proud of it. It's the same feeling as when a big shop closes on the high street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your buying would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Catalogue comparison and price checks, first. The planning of quantities after that. What stays is the choosing: which sofa, which shade, which shop owner needs a little extra help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you change your own role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train a younger buyer, Jonas, to do it with me. A person who knows both the tools and the shop owners will be worth a lot. I'd also be easier to keep if I'm the one who shows it works.

say: I'd say it's real change and we must **prepare the young**.
I'd say **test it properly** on small orders first.
think: Much of buying is **thinking work**, like comparing prices and checking catalogues.
Software is weaker on **taste**, but a manager might not see the difference.
do: Learn the tools **properly** once I've seen they work.
Focus on **spotting** what customers will like.
Save **350 a month** in case the firm cuts a senior buyer.
feel: **Uneasy**, like watching a big shop close on the high street.
S1.quote: A person who knows both the tools and the shop owners will be worth a lot.
fieldNote: She is **steady and proof-first**, willing to learn once the tools show results.
Her plan is to **teach a junior colleague**, so both of them become harder to replace.

steps.text: Try the planning tools on one small range first
Train Jonas to buy with me using the tools and the shop owners
Save 350 a month in case the firm cuts a senior buyer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast. At church I'd say we must look after each other. At work I'd say the firm must tell us the plan. Online, I'd say the people building this should answer for how fast it's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd say my buying job is gone by 2028. Choosing and planning are thinking work and AI does it. The robots arrive three years later for the warehouses and the delivery vans. Our shops would suffer too, because the shop owners would use AI to order straight from the factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down with Martin and cut our spending. I'd ask the firm about early retirement or a payout, and I'd learn the tools better so I stay useful. I'd also ask whether I could move into advising shops. Shop owners will need someone they trust, and that could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not panic, but I'd feel the weight. We have five months in the bank and a workshop that doesn't earn much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Martin, we've been through lean years and we'll go through this. We'd cut the holiday, the new kitchen, and maybe sell the caravan. I'd ask him to look for more commissions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Martin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to our pastor and my sister. I wouldn't ask for money, but it helps to speak to people who know you. And I'd write down what I know about the shops, so it's useful to someone.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the builders should answer for it.
At church I'd say we must **look after** each other.
think: My buying job is **gone by 2028**, since choosing and planning are thinking work.
Shops may order straight from factories, so our **shops suffer** too.
do: Sit down with Martin and **cut our spending**.
Ask the firm about **early retirement** or a payout.
feel: **Anxious**, feeling the weight, with five months in the bank.
S2.quote: Shop owners will need someone they trust, and that could be me.
fieldNote: She is **anxious but resourceful**, seeing a future as a trusted adviser to the shops.
The **couple's weak income base** (his workshop, her five months' savings) drives her caution.

steps.text: Sit down with Martin and cut the holiday, kitchen and caravan
Ask the firm about early retirement or a payout
Offer advice to the shops I know well
Talk with our pastor and my sister for support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if we start now. At work I'd say train juniors properly, with apprenticeships. At church I'd say pray and prepare. I'd say we shouldn't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it still bothers me. I'd be 63, I'd have worked for forty years, and I'd be told my skills are worth little. The time helps me fix the money, and I'm glad of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build savings to eight months, finish paying the car, and help Martin move to more profitable work. I'd learn the tools well, so I can offer advice to shops. By year four, I'd be part-time with the firm and start my own advising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Five years is like knowing winter is coming, so you stock the cellar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is better than two. What changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly. Shop owners value trust more than speed, and I've got thirty years of it. Some will pay for it, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass on what I know to Jonas and the younger buyers. It's the right thing to do, and it makes me feel less like a leftover.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if we start now, and firms must act.
I'd say train juniors properly through **apprenticeships**.
think: Even at 63 after forty years, I'd be told my skills are **worth little**.
The time helps me **fix the money**, and I'm glad.
do: Build savings to **eight months** and finish paying the car.
Help Martin move to more **profitable work**.
Go **part-time** by year four and start advising shops.
feel: **Anxious**, but steady, like stocking the cellar for winter.
S3.quote: Five years is like knowing winter is coming, so you stock the cellar.
fieldNote: She uses the extra time to **fix household money** and prepare an advising role.
She wants to **pass on her knowledge**, which keeps her from feeling like a leftover.

steps.text: Build savings to eight months and finish paying the car
Help Martin shift to more profitable commissions
Learn the tools well enough to advise shops
Go part-time by year four and start advising

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it well, with proper apprenticeships and savings schemes. At church I'd say we should teach the young to work with their hands and with their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68 and retired. It's not me I worry for. I worry for my nephew who's starting as a buyer and for the little shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 62 or 63 and retire. I'd keep a small advisory role if shops asked. I'd also help Martin's workshop, since I'd have more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly for others. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What's different for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn the tools early, keep their shop owners' trust, save from the first payslip, and look after their health. And to be kind. People remember it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small mentoring group for the new buyers. We'd meet monthly and talk through orders. It's a small thing, but it builds something.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** to do it well with apprenticeships and savings schemes.
At church I'd say teach the young to work with **hands** and heads.
think: I'd be **68 and retired**, so I worry for my nephew and the little shops.
do: Keep a small **advisory role** for shops that ask.
Start a **mentoring group** with Jonas for new buyers.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for others, and sleeping fine.
S4.quote: I'd start a small mentoring group for the new buyers. We'd meet monthly and talk through orders.
fieldNote: With ten years her concern is **for her nephew** and the little shops, not for herself.
She wants **mentoring** as a legacy, consistent with her traditional values of kindness and craft.

steps.text: Start a monthly mentoring group for new buyers
Keep a small advisory role for shops that ask

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to line up what we'd need. I'm 58, we have about five months saved, and Martin, my husband, runs a small carpentry workshop that isn't growing. What would help is honest notice from the firm and fair terms on my pension. I'd also want young people to have real apprenticeships, since they're the ones with the longest road.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm no enemy of progress, though I'm not a cheerleader either. I'll use what's proven, and I'll tell the truth about what I see.

headlineQuote: I'm no enemy of progress, though I'm not a cheerleader either. I'll use what's proven, and I'll tell the truth about what I see.
portrait: **Esther** is 58, a senior buyer of furniture and homeware for a distributor serving about four hundred independent shops.
She is **steady** and open to change once it is proven, using AI tools now and then.
Traditional and pro-market, she values **work, church and family**, and blames online marketplaces and short-term boards.
With about **five months saved** and a husband whose carpentry workshop isn't growing, money is tight at the edges.
She feels calm in a slow world and grows **anxious** as the date comes closer.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, since there'd be no time to line up what her household needs.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **honest notice** from the firm, fair pension terms and real apprenticeships for the young.
